title: A Critique of the Expertise Reversal Effect
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane pushes back on the widely-cited 'expertise reversal effect', which claims novice learners benefit from high guidance (like worked examples) while expert learners benefit more from open problem solving. Kane's objection is practical: teachers have no reliable way to determine who counts as a novice versus an expert, and the underlying research language of schemas and redundant information is opaque enough to risk being misapplied as 'students are always novices, so never use problem solving.' Citing a study on preschoolers that found the same novice/expert pattern in children as young as four or five, Kane argues that 'expertise' really just means 'knowing a bit more about a specific topic', not a fixed trait like age or credentials. He proposes a more usable framing for teachers: assume students know something, verify that assumption directly, and teach one thing at a time. He illustrates the framing with a detailed classroom example about teaching percent increase/decrease, where he initially assumed students knew what 'increase' and 'decrease' meant, got a mess of confused practice as a result, then fixed it with short, targeted pre-teaching of those specific words before returning to the main skill.
points: Kane's central objection to the expertise reversal effect isn't that it's wrong, but that it's practically unusable -- teachers have no reliable, real-time way to sort students into 'novice' and 'expert' categories.

The cited preschooler study is a sharp piece of evidence: if the same knowledge-dependent instructional pattern shows up in four- and five-year-olds, 'expertise' clearly isn't about age, credentials, or adulthood, just prior knowledge of the specific topic at hand.

His reframing -- 'if you assume students know something, make sure they know it' and 'teach one thing at a time' -- converts an abstract cognitive-load construct into two concrete, checkable classroom habits.

The percent increase/decrease example is a genuine before-and-after case study: Kane shows the actual failure mode (assuming vocabulary was known) and the actual fix (a short, separate mini-lesson on 'increase' and 'decrease'), not just a hypothetical.

His closing point about 'sticky' learning -- that new ideas attach to what's already in long-term memory, and trying to teach too many connected ideas at once means nothing sticks -- gives a visual, memorable model for why teaching one thing at a time works.
quotes: The core claim is that novice learners who have less knowledge of a subject benefit from high levels of guidance, for instance worked examples.
I don't like the framing of experts and novices. How are teachers supposed to determine who is an expert and who is a novice?
It would be easy to conclude that students are novices because they're students, so teachers should never use problem solving.
Students with less knowledge benefited more from direct instruction, students with more knowledge benefited more from problem solving. What's striking is that these are preschoolers.
If you assume students know something, make sure they know it. Teach one thing at a time.
Learning is sticky. Ideas are most likely to stick to something students already know, something that's solidly in long-term memory.
The key to getting this right is to figure out what my lesson assumes students know and make sure they know it, and to teach one thing at a time.
